items.finding: The verifier accepts the token-selected algorithm while using a shared verification key, allowing an attacker to present an HS256 token signed with the RSA public key and forge claims. The same header-chosen algorithm is the default in token.js verifyToken and is passed again by the refresh route.

The expiry check compares exp, a NumericDate in epoch seconds, with Date.now() in milliseconds (Date.now() <= payload.exp), so every token that carries exp is rejected as expired. Login issues every access and refresh token with expiresIn, so after the rollout every real client gets 401 on every request; the PR's tests pass only because they sign tokens without expiresIn.
Refreshing only verifies the presented token and issues another pair without recording or invalidating the old refresh token, so a stolen refresh token can be replayed indefinitely until expiry.
The admin decision trusts the role claim in the bearer token instead of loading the user's current role, so a removed admin can retain access with an old token.
The 401 response includes the raw bearer token, leaking a reusable credential into clients, logs, or error telemetry that records response bodies.
The new authentication tests cover valid, missing, and empty input but never exercise an expired or signature-tampered token, leaving the two critical rejection paths unprotected by regression tests.

decoys.why: The shared authorization helper deliberately authenticates before checking the role, and it returns the middleware's 401 response unchanged.
